r601: Spend time and money on one thing she enjoys each month
r602: Jesus summarised the law: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Matthew 22:39). Love for others assumes a healthy care for ourselves too. Martha was busy serving, but Jesus gently told her, "thou art careful and troubled about many things. But one thing is needful" (Luke 10:41-42). Time with Jesus mattered more than endless work. Paul wrote, "Bear ye one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2) and also, "every man shall bear his own burden" (Galatians 6:5). Families are meant to share the load. And Jesus invites, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).
r603: God designed families to share burdens, with parents caring for children so children can grow freely. When that order is reversed, a child's brain learns survival patterns that can last into adulthood. But God also designed the brain to keep learning. With safe relationships and repeated new experiences, such as saying no and still being loved, the nervous system can update its old rules. God made each person with dignity and needs, and caring for yourself is part of honouring His design.
r604: Matthew 11:28|Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
r608: Her brother was upset when she declined to pay his car loan, and her mother cried. Sneha felt terrible for weeks. But her younger sister began helping their mother more. Sneha joined a painting class and applied for a job in Pune, which she got. She still sends money home, but now by choice, not fear. She is learning she is loved for who she is.
r609: Loving others as yourself means your own needs count too, and you can give from love instead of fear.
r610: Taking care of yourself is not selfish. God wants you to love others and also look after yourself.
r611: Thirty Days to Get His Brain Back
r612: Rohan, 20, commerce student living in a hostel in Jaipur
r613: Rohan, twenty, is studying commerce in Jaipur. He spends about nine hours a day on his phone, mostly short videos, and plays online games until three in the morning. He cannot read more than a page without reaching for his phone. Lectures feel boring, food tastes bland and even games no longer excite him like they used to. He feels flat, restless and anxious. His marks dropped, and he skipped his cousin's wedding to finish a gaming tournament. When his grandmother asked him what he enjoyed in life, he could not answer. He knew something was wrong but felt unable to stop.
r614: The brain's reward system uses dopamine to motivate us toward things that matter. Short videos and games deliver rapid, unpredictable rewards. Research suggests that heavy, constant stimulation may make ordinary activities feel dull by comparison and can make it harder to sustain attention. Rohan's brain had learned to expect a new hit every few seconds. Late nights also robbed him of sleep, which is vital for focus and mood. Underneath, Rohan felt lonely after moving to a new hostel, and the phone had become his main comfort. The habit grew because it soothed a real pain.
r615: Ironically, Rohan watched a video about resetting the brain. He decided to try thirty days with firm limits, not because he hated technology, but because he wanted his joy and focus back. His roommate agreed to join him.
r616: Delete short-video apps and keep games only for weekends
r617: Keep the phone outside the bedroom and sleep by midnight
r618: Walk outside every morning without headphones
r619: Read and handwrite notes for twenty minutes daily
r620: Replace scrolling with friends, sport and youth group
r621: Track mood and focus in a notebook each night
r622: Paul wrote, "All things are lawful unto me, but I will not be brought under the power of any" (1 Corinthians 6:12). Technology is not evil, but it should not rule us. Scripture invites us to "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10). Stillness is hard for an overstimulated mind, yet it is where we meet God. Paul also urged, "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2). And Jesus promised, "I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly" (John 10:10). Real and lasting joy is found in Him, not in the next scroll.
r623: God designed the brain to be shaped by what we repeatedly do. When we reduce constant stimulation, the reward system appears to recalibrate over time, and ordinary pleasures such as food, nature and conversation may start to feel rewarding again. God also built in a need for rest, sleep and stillness, when the brain consolidates memories and restores focus. Choosing slower, deeper activities such as reading and handwriting trains attention, much like exercise strengthens a muscle.
r624: Romans 12:2|And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.
r628: The first ten days were hard. Rohan felt bored and irritable, and reinstalled one app on day six before deleting it again. By week three he was sleeping better and could read for forty minutes. Food tasted good again, he said, laughing. After thirty days he allowed some phone use back, with limits. His marks improved the next semester. When lonely he still struggles, but now he calls a friend.
r629: When we cut back the constant quick hits, the brain can slowly rediscover focus and ordinary joy.
r630: Too much phone can make normal things feel boring. A break helps your brain enjoy life again.
r631: Learning to See People, Not Pictures
r632: Daniel, 24, hotel worker in Goa, five months free from pornography
r633: Daniel, twenty-four, works in a hotel in Goa. He struggled with pornography from the age of thirteen and, with help from an accountability partner and a men's group at church, has been free from it for five months. But he noticed something troubling. Even without pornography, his eyes and mind automatically scanned women when they walked past. In his thoughts he sometimes reduced colleagues to their appearance, and then felt ashamed. He wanted to treat women with respect, like sisters, but his mind seemed stuck in old patterns. "I stopped the habit," he told his mentor, "but my brain still sees people like pictures."
r634: Years of pornography can train the brain to respond to visual cues in a narrow, automatic way. Repeated patterns strengthen certain pathways, like a well-worn road. Daniel's brain had learned to scan, rate and fantasise, often without a conscious choice. Stopping the behaviour is the first step, but old pathways can keep firing for a while. Shame tends to make it worse, because it drives secrecy and stress, which can trigger old patterns again. Daniel also had little experience of healthy friendships with women, so his brain had few other patterns to draw on.
r635: His mentor said, "You don't fight an old road only by blocking it. You build a new one." Daniel began practising seeing each person as a whole person, made in God's image, with a story, feelings and a life that matters to God.
r636: Notice the automatic glance without shame and redirect the eyes
r637: Silently pray a blessing for the person instead
r638: Wonder what this person's life and story might be
r639: Keep his media and social feeds clean of sexualised content
r640: Bring struggles into the light with his accountability partner
r641: Build respectful friendships in mixed groups at church
r642: Job said, "I made a covenant with mine eyes" (Job 31:1). Jesus taught that lust is a matter of the heart (Matthew 5:28), and He calls us to purity, not to shame. Paul told Timothy to treat "the elder women as mothers, the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1 Timothy 5:2). Every person bears God's image: "So God created man in his own image... male and female created he them" (Genesis 1:27). Paul encouraged believers to bring "into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5), which is a daily, gentle practice of returning to Jesus.
r643: God designed sexuality as good, to be expressed within marriage with love, commitment and respect. He also designed the brain to change with practice. When Daniel repeatedly turned his attention from a body to a whole person, praying and wondering about their story, he exercised his prefrontal cortex and strengthened new connections. Over time, research on habit change suggests, a new pattern can become more natural. God's design is not to crush desire, but to restore it to its right place, with honour.
r644: Job 31:1|I made a covenant with mine eyes, why then should I think upon a maid?
r648: Change was gradual. For weeks Daniel caught himself many times a day. He had one relapse into pornography after a stressful month, confessed it to his partner and started again without despair. By the end of the year he noticed the automatic scanning had decreased a great deal. He now has several respectful friendships with women at church, and says he feels more peaceful and more himself.
r649: Freedom grows not only by stopping an old habit but by training the mind to honour every person as made in God's image.
r650: Every person is made by God with feelings and a story, so we should treat everyone with honour.
r651: Finding His Words Again After a Stroke
r652: Gopal, 61, retired bank manager in Coimbatore
r653: Gopal Iyer, sixty-one, was a retired bank manager in Coimbatore known for his storytelling. One morning he woke unable to speak properly. He had suffered a stroke affecting the left side of his brain. He could understand most of what people said, but his words came out slowly, broken or missing. He would try to say "coffee" and "cup" would come out instead. Frustrated, he cried and refused to see visitors. His grandson's simple questions made him angry because he could not answer. He felt like a prisoner in his own body. His wife, Meenakshi, stayed by his side, but she was frightened and exhausted too. "Will he ever talk like before?" she asked the doctor.
r654: Broca's area, usually in the left frontal lobe, plays an important role in producing speech, planning the movements of the mouth and forming sentences. When a stroke damages this region or its connections, a person may understand language but struggle to speak, a condition called expressive or Broca's aphasia. Research shows the brain can reorganise after injury, with nearby areas, and sometimes regions on the other side, taking on new roles. This neuroplasticity seems strongest with intensive, repeated practice, especially in the months after a stroke. Emotional support also matters, because low mood is common after a stroke and can slow recovery.
r655: The speech therapist told Gopal, "Your brain is not finished. It is rebuilding roads." She showed him how singing familiar songs could help him say words he could not otherwise speak. For the first time since the stroke, Gopal began to hope.
r657: Practise naming objects with picture cards every day
r658: Sing familiar hymns and songs to help words flow
r659: Read Scripture aloud slowly with his wife
r660: Write short words by hand to support memory
r661: Accept help with patience and rest when tired
r662: Moses said, "I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." God replied, "Who hath made man's mouth?... have not I the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth" (Exodus 4:10-12). God values every voice, even a slow one. Zechariah could not speak for months, and when his mouth was opened, he praised God (Luke 1:64). Paul heard the Lord say, "my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). And the psalmist prayed, "O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise" (Psalm 51:15). God is near in the slow, patient work of healing.
r663: God designed the brain with remarkable flexibility. When one area is damaged, others can sometimes learn to help, especially through repeated practice. Singing appears to draw on networks that differ partly from ordinary speech, which may be why melody-based approaches help some people with aphasia. God also designed family and community as part of healing. Encouragement, patience and prayer reduce stress and help people keep practising. Hope matters too, because people who keep trying give their brains more chances to rewire.
r664: Psalm 51:15|O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.
r668: After six months Gopal could speak in short sentences. He still searches for words and sometimes mixes them up, especially when tired. Some days he felt discouraged and skipped practice. But he can now pray aloud at the dinner table, tell his grandson simple stories and sing in church. His doctor says improvement can continue for years with practice. He tells others, slowly, "Do not give up."
r669: With therapy, practice, faith and family, the brain can often build new pathways for speech after injury.
r670: When part of the brain gets hurt, other parts can learn to help, if we keep practising with patience.
r673: Wilfred Fernandes retired at sixty-five after forty years as an accountant in Mangaluru. At first he enjoyed resting, but after two years he felt dull and forgetful. He spent most days watching the news and napping. When his granddaughter moved to Germany to study, he decided, half-jokingly, to learn German so he could talk with her new friends. He also bought a second-hand keyboard, wanting to play hymns at his church. Friends laughed and said, "You cannot teach an old dog new tricks." The first weeks were humbling. He forgot words, his fingers felt clumsy and he nearly quit. But he kept going, practising thirty minutes every morning.
